Sourcing: 45 of the 60 come from facts with timesUsed 0 (the untapped pool). The remaining 15 use timesUsed>=1 facts at a deliberately different angle from alreadyAsked — e.g. run 1 asked "What was the Bulls' record in 1995-96?", mine asks which team went 72-10; run 1 asked how many points Wilt scored... (who holds the single-game record), mine asks the number itself at t:0; run 1 asked which jersey number Jordan wore on his comeback, mine asks for the two-word statement.

Calibration notes:
- t:0 leans on the permitted helpers: the question often echoes or frames the answer ("their oldest rivals", "Golden State guard famous for launching from way behind the line"), and distractors are often cross-era or absurd (Dennis Rodman/Ben Wallace as three-point leaders, "driving the team bus", "Anchorage, Alaska"). Numeric t:0 answers use far-apart distractors (100/62/81/150; 18/22/25/29).
- t:1 never hands over the answer and every distractor is a real, era-correct候 candidate: 1990 Finals MVP distractors are all Bad Boys Pistons; 1999 Spurs FMVP distractors are all Spurs; 2003 draft distractors are all teams that picked in that top five.
- Volatile flags set on the four genuinely chase-able items: LeBron's career scoring record, Curry's three-point record, Westbrook's triple-double record, and the Lakers' 33-game streak. Settled history (Jordan 6-0, Wilt's 100, Warriors' 73 wins, Barkley never scoring 70) is not flagged.
- Deliberately avoided at both tiers: obscure Finals MVPs (Unseld, Maxwell, Dennis Johnson), quadruple-double trivia, and pre-1960 franchise history — run 1 already mined those and they cannot be written down to an easy bar honestly.
- Skipped facts I judged unusable at these tiers even though unused: nba-1951-rochester-royals-title, nba-wilt-fg-pct-727, nba-wilt-35-straight-fg, nba-baylor-71-1960, nba-hakeem-quad — all require recall a casual fan simply does not have, and padding them into t:1 would have made that tier dishonest.

Dedupe discipline: every re-angled fact yields a different ANSWER than the version in alreadyAsked (e.g. asked "who coined 'slam dunk'" → mine asks which team he called games for; asked "which official judged the ball" → mine asks the umpire's duty; asked "flagrant 1 vs 2" → mine asks the penalty). I dropped a planned cherry-picking t:0 because it would have been the asked question inverted, and swapped in the Chris Ford/Celtics item instead. any-foul-charge-vs-block and any-scoring-two-and-three-points are the only facts used twice, with distinct answers (charge at t:0, block at t:1).

Nothing here is volatile — the corpus contains no active-player totals or live records; the ABA, rules and dimensions facts are all settled history, so volatile is omitted (false) throughout. Two questions land on 1949 (any-origins-baa-1946-nba-1949) as an answer but come from different facts and different angles.

A handful of facts I deliberately skipped as unusable at these tiers: the lead/trail/center officiating mechanics, Hawkins' 26.8 ppg, court and backboard measurements — all require recall no casual fan has, and padding easy tiers with them would just be mislabeled hard questions.

Distractors there deliberately pull from other sports (Seahawks, Yankees, Colts) or are far-apart numbers, per the t:0 license.

- volatile:true set only where the fact can genuinely go stale: active-player totals and chased records (Clark assists, Reese rebounding average, Griner blocks, Wilson MVP count, Taurasi's gold-medal count, Reeve's win record), plus the still-shifting expansion items (Detroit 2029, 15-team count) and the ongoing USA gold streak. kills.q: In a triangle-and-two defense, how many defenders are guarding an opponent man-to-man?
kills.reason: Giveaway at t:1 — the answer is literally embedded in the defense's name. The naming convention for junk defenses is [zone shape]-and-[number of man-to-man defenders] (box-and-one, triangle-and-two, diamond-and-one), so a player with zero basketball knowledge just reads 'two' out of the question text and picks 'Two'. No knowledge is required at a tier that is supposed to demand some. (The marked answer is factually correct — two man defenders, three in a zone triangle — it just isn't a real question. Could be salvaged by asking the inverse, e.g. 'A box-and-one and a triangle-and-two both leave how many defenders playing zone?')

kills.q: Which Harlem Globetrotter was billed as the 'Clown Prince of Basketball'?
kills.reason: Ambiguous — a listed distractor is also defensibly correct. Reece 'Goose' Tatum is the ORIGINAL 'Clown Prince of Basketball' (Wikipedia's lede on Tatum: 'nicknamed the Clown Prince of Basketball'; Black Fives and Hall of Fame bios use the same title). Meadowlark Lemon inherited the billing when he took over as chief showman after Tatum. With both Lemon and Tatum among the four choices there is no defensible single answer.

fixes.q: In 2006 a Lakers guard scored 81 points in one game against Toronto — the second-highest total in NBA history. Who was he?
fixes.problem: The premise is now factually wrong. On March 10, 2026 Bam Adebayo scored 83 for Miami vs. Washington, pushing Kobe's 81 down to THIRD-highest (Wilt 100, Adebayo 83, Kobe 81). This set even contains the Adebayo 83 question, so the two questions directly contradict each other. Reword the stem to '...the third-highest total in NBA history' (or drop the ranking clause entirely: 'In 2006 a Lakers guard scored 81 points in one game against Toronto. Who was he?'). The keyed answer, Kobe Bryant, stays correct.
fixes.correctAnswer: Kobe Bryant — but stem must read 'third-highest total in NBA history' (or omit the ranking)

fixes.q: Which Minnesota Lynx coach tied Mike Thibault's WNBA record for career regular-season wins in 2026?
fixes.problem: Stale/imprecise premise. Reeve did not merely tie the record — on July 8, 2026 she won her 380th regular-season game to PASS Thibault's 379 and become the outright winningest coach in WNBA history. As written (today is 2026-07-25) the question describes a moment that has already been superseded. The answer choice itself is unaffected.
fixes.correctAnswer: Cheryl Reeve — reword to: 'Which Minnesota Lynx coach passed Mike Thibault in 2026 to become the winningest head coach in WNBA history?'

fixes.q: Sue Bird spent her entire 20-year WNBA career with which Seattle team?
fixes.problem: The '20-year' figure is wrong in both readings: Bird was drafted in 2002 and retired after 2022 (a 21-season span) but missed 2013 and 2019 to injury, so she actually played 19 seasons. Answer choice is unaffected (t:0, Seattle Storm is obviously right), but the stated number is inaccurate.
fixes.correctAnswer: Seattle Storm — reword to 'spent her entire WNBA career (2002-2022) with which Seattle team?'

fixes.q: Who was named Finals MVP as the Los Angeles Sparks won the 2016 WNBA championship?
fixes.problem: No answer change needed, but flagging a trap: the srcId is 'wnba-2016-ogwumike-mvp', which refers to Nneka Ogwumike winning the 2016 REGULAR-SEASON MVP — a different award, and Ogwumike is listed as a distractor. Candace Parker (c[0]) is the correct 2016 Finals MVP (28 pts, 12 reb in Game 5). Do not let a later pass 'correct' this to Ogwumike; consider repointing the srcId.

fixes.q: Patty Mills scored 42 points in a bronze medal game to win a first ever Olympic basketball medal for which country?
fixes.problem: The answer (Australia) is correct and unambiguous, but the premise is factually loose: Tokyo 2020 was Australia's first Olympic MEN'S basketball medal. The Australian women (the Opals) had already won silver in 2000, 2004 and 2008 and bronze in 1996 and 2012, so it was not the country's 'first ever Olympic basketball medal'. Reword to 'a first ever Olympic men's basketball medal'.

fixes.q: During the 2023 NCAA tournament, Caitlin Clark became the first player in tournament history to do what in back-to-back games?
fixes.problem: The marked answer (Score 40 points) is what she did, but the stem's superlative is factually wrong as written. Notre Dame's Austin Carr scored 61, 52 and 45 in consecutive 1970 NCAA tournament games, so Clark was NOT the first player in NCAA tournament history to post back-to-back 40-point games — she was the first in WOMEN'S tournament history (41 vs. Louisville in the Elite Eight, 41 vs. South Carolina in the Final Four). Distractors are safe (her Louisville triple-double was a single game, not back-to-back).
fixes.correctAnswer: Score 40 points — but reword the stem to 'became the first player in women's NCAA tournament history to do what in back-to-back games?'

fixes.q: Carmelo Anthony's 33 points against Texas in the 2003 national semifinal set an NCAA tournament record for a player in which class?
fixes.problem: 'NCAA tournament record' over-claims. Every source describes the 33 points as the most ever scored by a freshman in a FINAL FOUR game, not an all-tournament freshman record (freshmen have gone higher in earlier rounds). The class answer itself is right — Anthony was a freshman one-and-done in 2003.
fixes.correctAnswer: Freshman — but reword the stem to 'set a Final Four record for a player in which class?'

fixes.q: Don Barksdale's United States team went a perfect 12-0 at the 1948 London Olympics. Which medal did they take home?
fixes.problem: The premise is factually wrong: the 1948 U.S. Olympic basketball team went 8-0, not 12-0 (five group games plus quarterfinal, semifinal and the 65-21 final over France). The marked answer 'Gold' is correct, so only the record needs correcting. Suggested rewrite: "Don Barksdale's United States team went a perfect 8-0 at the 1948 London Olympics. Which medal did they take home?"
